results.title: 3000-year-old copper smelting site reveals the dawn of iron age technology - AOL
results.content: # 3000-year-old copper smelting site reveals the dawn of iron age technology. Uncovered in the late 1950s, the Kvemo Bolnisi workshop was considered to be one of the Caucasus’s oldest iron smelting factories. Early reports described the picture of a stone furnace into a hillside fit, piles of hematite lying around the floor, and an enormous slag pile out back. A new look at the evidence shows that Kvemo Bolnisi wasn’t producing iron at all—it was a copper shop that used iron minerals in unexpected and creative ways. Because the floor of the workshop was smeared with hematite, an iron oxide, the site was labeled an early iron factory. Map of the South Caucasus showing the location of Kvemo Bolnisi and Colchis, a region with the well-documented LBA-EIA copper smelting landscapes discussed in the text. The addition of iron oxide to the furnace changed the slag chemistry so that it was more slippery and easier to take off molten copper. It’s evidence of intentional use of iron in copper smelting.

results.title: Extraction and separation of copper and iron from copper smelting slag: A review - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Extraction and separation of copper and iron from copper smelting slag: A review. A large amount of copper smelting slag (CSS) containing valuable elements such as copper and iron is produced through smelting. CSS is a kind of solid waste slag produced in the process of pyrometallurgical copper smelting (Piatak et al., 2015; Sarfo et al., 2017). The typical copper smelting process flow of chalcopyrite is shown in Fig. 1 (Tian et al., 2021). Consequently, it is imperative to realize the efficient development and utilization of CSS resources, improve the self-sufficiency rate of copper concentrate and iron concentrate, and strengthen environmental protection by strengthening independent technological innovation (Sarfo et al., 2017; Starodub et al., 2016; Wang, Zhu et al., 2022). This work mainly reviews and combs the physical separation methods, chemical separation methods and combined separation methods used to separate and extract copper and iron from CSS, and puts forward a new route to treat CSS by microwave fluidization roasting. In the smelting process, the composition of smelting slag will change greatly under different influencing factors (copper ore raw materials, flux, smelting mode, etc.). According to different copper smelting properties, various beneficiation and metallurgical methods were generally used to extract and recover valuable metals, including flotation, roasting followed by magnetic separation, leaching, smelting and other processes. ### Base metals recovery from copper smelter slag by oxidising leaching and solvent extraction. ### Green and efficient utilization of waste ferric-oxide desulfurizer to clean waste copper slag by the smelting reduction-sulfurizing process. ### Technological scheme for copper slag processing. ### Recovery of iron and removal of hazardous elements from waste copper slag via a novel aluminothermic smelting reduction (ASR) process. ### The pH-dependent leaching behavior of slags from various stages of a copper smelting process: environmental implications. ### A novel process to upgrade the copper slag by direct reduction-magnetic separation with the addition of Na2CO3 and CaO. ### Research status of iron recovery from copper slag and proposal of new methods. ### Recovery of value metals from copper smelter slag by ammonium chloride treatment. ### Characteristics and mechanism of reduction and smelting-separation process of copper slag. ### Cleaner recycling of iron from waste copper slag by using walnut shell char as green reductant.
